answer: The relational classifier uses the network's label distribution as a feature when the nodes' neighbors carry usable label information. This applies when (1) the network shows label autocorrelation or homophily, so linked nodes tend to share labels; (2) some neighbors' labels are known, either from training data or from earlier inference steps; and (3) node attributes alone are insufficient to classify accurately. In that case each node's feature vector combines its own attribute features with aggregated neighbor-label features, such as counts or proportions of each class among its neighbors. Mixing the two is necessary because attributes capture a node's intrinsic characteristics, while the neighbor label distribution captures the dependence between linked nodes that attributes miss. Using both generally yields better performance than either alone. When neighbor labels are unknown, methods such as collective classification estimate them iteratively, using the current label estimates as the relational features until they stabilize.
